lead: Light sometimes behaves as a particle with fixed energy and momentum, and sometimes as a wave. Matter does the same. Every moving particle has a matter wave of wavelength λ = h/p, where λ is in metres, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s is Planck's constant, and p is momentum in kg·m/s. This de Broglie relation connects particle momentum to wave length. It explains electron diffraction, guides electron microscopes, and marks where quantum effects matter. A cricket ball has a wavelength so tiny that its wave nature is unobservable.
prereq: You need: photon momentum from 6.2, wave ideas from Unit 2, and relativistic momentum from Unit 1 for high energies.

sections.h3: Wave and particle in one object

blocks.text: Light forces two pictures. A photon carries energy E = hν, where ν is frequency, and momentum p = h/λ; it can eject one electron in the photoelectric effect or share energy in Compton scattering (6.2). Yet light also shows interference and diffraction. The photon is one object, tested in two ways.

De Broglie reversed the question. A particle with momentum p has a matter wave of wavelength λ = h/p. A matter wave is the wave whose intensity gives the probability of finding the particle; it is not a ripple of material. Electron diffraction from a crystal confirms this wave for electrons.

blocks.where: λ is the de Broglie wavelength in metres; h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s is Planck's constant; p is momentum in kg·m/s; m is mass in kg; v is speed in m/s. For a photon, p = h/λ = E/c, where c is the speed of light.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this wave properties of particles. The same relation covers photons and electrons; only the momentum expression changes.

For a slow electron accelerated from rest through V volts, the electric energy eV becomes kinetic energy p²/(2m), where e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is the elementary charge. So p = √(2meV). Planck's relation then gives λ = h/√(2meV).

blocks.where: V is the accelerating voltage in volts; λ is in ångström (1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m). This nonrelativistic form is accurate when the electron energy is much less than 511 keV.

blocks.text: At 100 V, λ = 12.27/√100 = 1.227 Å = 0.123 nm. A cricket ball of mass 0.16 kg moving at 30 m/s has p = 4.8 kg·m/s, so λ = 1.4 × 10⁻³⁴ m. That is far below any measurable slit, so its wave nature is invisible. The electron wavelength is comparable to atomic spacing, so crystals diffract electrons. At electron energies near 511 keV, use relativistic momentum from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Electron double slit and what λ means

blocks.text: Fire electrons one at a time at two narrow slits. Each electron arrives as one localized dot, yet many dots build an interference pattern. The fringe spacing depends on λ = h/p. This is wave-particle duality in one experiment: the electron is detected as a particle and guided by a matter wave.

If a detector records which slit each electron used, the pattern changes to two broad bands. The wave description needs both paths; knowing the path destroys the interference. This is why the wave is not a hidden push on a classical particle.

Do not read λ as the size of the electron. It is the wavelength of the probability amplitude, developed in 6.6. Large momentum means short wavelength and more particle-like behaviour. The double-slit test with electrons is the cleanest classroom picture; crystal diffraction is the usual laboratory proof, covered in 6.4.

figure.caption: Wave properties (interference, diffraction) and particle properties (momentum, a localized hit) overlap in the de Broglie relation λ = h/p. Notice that the relation uses momentum, not energy alone.

spec.aria: A Venn diagram of wave properties and particle properties; the overlap holds de Broglie's relation λ = h/p.

examples.question: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 100 V. Find its de Broglie wavelength. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
steps: Kinetic energy gained: K = eV = (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(100 V) = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁷ J.
Nonrelativistic momentum: p = √(2mK) = √(2 × 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁷ J) = 5.40 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s.
De Broglie wavelength: λ = h/p = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)/(5.40 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s) = 1.228 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.
Convert: λ = 0.1228 nm = 1.228 Å, which rounds to 0.123 nm = 1.23 Å.
examples.answer: The de Broglie wavelength is 1.23 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, or 0.123 nm, or 1.23 Å.
examples.check:
import math
h = 6.63e-34
m = 9.11e-31
e = 1.60e-19
V = 100
p = math.sqrt(2*m*e*V)
lam = h/p
print(f'{lam:.2e}')
print(f'{lam*1e9:.3f}')
print(f'{lam*1e10:.2f}')

traps: Using p = mv at high voltage. When kinetic energy approaches 511 keV for an electron, use relativistic p = γmv; the low-voltage formula fails.
Do not mix volts and electron-volts. V in λ = 12.27/√V Å is volts; energy eV is in joules when e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
λ is not the size of the particle. It is the matter-wave wavelength; an electron can have λ larger than its own classical radius.
For a proton or ion, replace m and charge in p = √(2mqV); 12.27/√V Å is only for electrons.

quiz.q: State de Broglie's relation for a matter wave and define each symbol.
quiz.a: λ = h/p; λ is wavelength in m, h is Planck's constant 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, and p is momentum in kg·m/s.

quiz.q: Why is the de Broglie wavelength of a cricket ball not observed?
quiz.a: Its momentum is large, so λ is about 10⁻³⁴ m, far smaller than any slit or detector; diffraction is negligible.

quiz.q: An electron is accelerated through 400 V. Find its de Broglie wavelength nonrelativistically.
If the momentum of a particle doubles, what happens to its de Broglie wavelength and to its wave-like visibility?
quiz.a: λ halves. A shorter wavelength gives narrower interference fringes, so wave effects become harder to observe.

quiz.q: Give one experiment showing light as a particle and one showing light as a wave.
quiz.a: Photoelectric effect or Compton scattering shows particle behaviour; interference or diffraction shows wave behaviour.

quiz.q: In an electron double-slit experiment, a detector identifies which slit each electron passes through. Describe the pattern.
quiz.a: The interference fringes disappear. Two single-slit bands remain because path knowledge removes the phase relation between the two paths.

beyond: Not for the exam. Electron microscopes use short de Broglie wavelengths to resolve objects smaller than visible light allows. Neutron and atom interferometers use matter waves to sense rotation and gravity. Modern experiments send large molecules through gratings and still see interference. Search next for matter-wave interferometry, electron diffraction, and atom interferometer.
